books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, A. Reform Movements in the Antebellum Period

stimulus.text: "Education, then, beyond all other devices of human origin, is the great equalizer of the conditions of men, — the balance-wheel of the social machinery. . . . It does better than to disarm the poor of their hostility towards the rich: it prevents being poor." — Horace Mann, Twelfth Annual Report to the Massachusetts Board of Education, 1848
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Horace Mann, Twelfth Annual Report of the Secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education (1848). Wording checked against the report text as reprinted in Life and Works of Horace Mann, vol. III (1868), p. 669, and the ETSU faculty transcription; ellipses mark omissions.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Mann, Twelfth Annual Report (1848)
stem: Which of the following criticisms of Mann's common schools is best supported by the books?

options.text: Catholic families feared Protestant teaching in the schools
Whigs opposed all public spending on schools
options.misconception: Whigs favored an active government and public improvements, including schools.

options.text: Mann wanted schools to teach only religion
options.misconception: Mann's schools taught reading, writing, arithmetic, and morals — not religion alone.

options.text: Southern planters funded the Massachusetts schools
options.misconception: Massachusetts paid for its own schools; Southern planters had no part in funding them.

rationales.A: The books record that Catholic families worried public-school instruction would include Protestant indoctrination. The fear was real and widely shared.
rationales.B: Whigs backed an active government that built schools, canals, and banks. Opposing school spending was the Democrats' line, not the Whigs'.
rationales.C: Mann's common schools taught the three Rs, history, and morals. Religion alone was never the curriculum.
rationales.D: Massachusetts taxpayers funded the common schools. Southern planters neither paid for them nor supported them.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who objected. The books name Catholic families, not Whigs or planters.
2. Ask what they feared. A public school teaching Protestant morals would indoctrinate their children.
3. See the limit. Even a reform for all children met resistance from families it meant to include.
Background: Critics also said moral education belonged to parents, not to the government.
Remember: a reform's critics tell you its limits — ask who felt left out and why.
